newsitem.title: USA: COMEX copper ends at 6-mth low on weak demand.
newsitem.headline: COMEX copper ends at 6-mth low on weak demand.

text.p: COMEX copper collapsed under the weight of increasingly weak fundamentals and the breakthough of key chart points to lead to the lowest price in six months.

The market is in the depth of the summer doldrums with London Metal Exchange warehouse stocks increasing steadily over the last two months to the highest level since September 1996, reflecting sluggish demand worldwide.
The LME cash-to-three-month spread evaporated to a $3 contango/$2 backwardation from as much as $250 a month ago.

"We've seen a sharp increase in stocks," said Michael Frawley, senior vice president of Dean Witter Reynolds. "The summer doldrums are upon us. I would expect to see this market on the defensive for the next three to four weeks. After that, ultimately we're looking at a good buying opportunity."
Physical traders agree that the market is looking increasingly sluggish. "There's plenty of copper around, and more arriving from Chile, Peru and Brazil every day," one said.

"The producers have excess copper to sell," another trader said. "The rod mills have essentially stopped buying spot metal. The brass mills are only buying bits and pieces. Plus Kennecott is coming back on line and we're starting to see them out and about."
Kennecott Utah Copper, a subsidiary of Rio Tinto, is in the process of bringing its 280,000-tonne-per-year Bingham Canyon smelter back from two years of production problems.

On the technical side, the picture looks even more bleak, brokers said. The neck-line of a head-and-shoulders pattern is emerging in the weekly September chart was broken at 101.50 cents a lb, according to a market report from GNI, suggesting that the next target on the downside is 84.00 cents a lb.

In other news, in the last two trading days, approximately 3,158 tonnes of copper have arrived in both the COMEX and LME warehouses in Baltimore from South America, in what many players believe is the beginning of a possible arbitrage play.

"The bottom line is that demand isn't strong enough to absorb all of the metal coming in from South America," said one physical trader. "So if they park the metal in Baltimore, maybe they can make some money playing the arbitrage (by shipping between the two warehouses)."
The LME cash price is currently trading at approximately 3.10 cents over the COMEX spot price, up from 0.50 cents for the better part of the week.
((--Derek J. Caney, New York Commodity Desk, 212-859-1646))
